name: congruence descent: rewriting under an application is done by rewriting arguments independently and assembling the proof from a congruence lemma that is synthesised on demand, with user-supplied congruence lemmas taking precedence

questions.ancestry: Lean 4 simp. Congruence closure for rewriting under binders/applications with dependent types is the specimen's most Lean-specific machinery; ancestry to Lean 3 simp's congr lemmas is T2.
questions.mechanism: To rewrite f a1 .. an: if a user congruence lemma is registered for f, try it (its hypotheses tell which arguments may be rewritten and under what extra local hypotheses, 552-585); else if no argument depends on another, rewrite each argument and chain mkCongr/mkCongrArg (fast path); else synthesise a congruence theorem for f from its type (which arguments are fixed, which can be rewritten by Eq, which need a cast because later types depend on them, which are subsingleton instances), cache it, and use it. The function position itself is also simplified (visitFn).
questions.input: an application Expr; the congruence store; the function's type for synthesis
questions.output: Result for the application with a proof assembled from the sub-results
questions.state: State.congrCache (per head function); reads the @[congr] extension; introduces local hypotheses while rewriting under dependent positions (the 'contextual' mode of user congr lemmas)
questions.assumptions: dependent type theory: rewriting an argument can change the TYPE of later arguments, hence casts and the fixed/eq/cast classification; that a congruence theorem can be synthesised for any function from its type alone
questions.interface: congr(e: Expr) -> SimpM Result; registerable user lemmas by head constant; the auto-synthesis is a pure function of the head's type (memoised)
questions.fitness_value: It is what makes 'rewrite anywhere inside the term' sound in a dependently typed setting; without it simp could rewrite only at the root or in non-dependent positions. Claimed from structure; not measured.
questions.failure_landscape: (a) an argument classified 'fixed' (because something depends on it) is never rewritten -- a silent completeness hole that user @[congr] lemmas exist to patch; (b) synthesis cost per new head function (cached, but first-hit); (c) Prop arguments and instance arguments are handled by special cases (subsingleton), which is a policy; (d) the interplay with proof-term size: every level of descent adds a congruence application to the proof.
questions.ablation: Designed, not measured: disable descent into applications (treat every app as atomic). Prediction: only root rewrites; virtually every mathlib simp call fails. Sharper: disable user @[congr] lemmas only and count which mathlib tests break -- a measurable fraction of the store's value that lives in hand-written congruence lemmas.
questions.decomposability: Into (1) the argument-kind classifier (fixed/eq/cast/heq/subsingletonInst -- the dependent-type-specific core), (2) the theorem synthesiser that emits a lemma from a classification, (3) the dispatcher that prefers user lemmas. In a simply-typed substrate (1) collapses to 'everything is eq' and the whole organ degenerates to structural recursion -- which is the honest transfer story.
questions.composability: Only substrates with dependent types or with positions that must not be rewritten need this; for Proteus boolean trees it is structural recursion. Its transferable residue is the IDEA of a per-head-symbol table saying which positions are rewritable, which any rule engine can host.
questions.human_prior: That equality is the relation rewriting preserves (a generalisation to arbitrary relations is what mathlib's gcongr does elsewhere, out of scope); that instance positions are irrelevant (subsingleton).
questions.control: Positive: f (a + 0) rewrites to f a under a rule a + 0 = a for an ordinary f. Negative: a position that later arguments depend on is left alone and the run does not error. Cheat control: an implementation that rewrites dependent positions anyway must be caught by the kernel (type error) -- so the control needs a kernel check of the produced proof, which means executing Lean. None executed in CUT-1.
questions.cheat: Rewriting everywhere and letting the kernel reject ill-typed proofs late would pass any test that only compares result terms; the control checks the proof, not the term.
